doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: Upcoming harp trio project and Satori's drummers
summary: She discusses the Maria-Christina Harper trio tour and album, and how James Maddren's absence is handled in Satori.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: What’s up for you next? Do you find that you need to shift from project to project depending on the availability of the people you play with?

Yeah. Actually up next is something I’m – it is a collaboration but it’s under the harp player’s name. There’s a harpist called Maria-Christina Harper oddly enough. She’s a Greek musician. And we started playing together about four years ago and we have a trio with me on saxophone and a drummer. And the drummer is in a couple of bands that are on tour a lot. So actually the next project I’m doing is we have an album release at the end of this month so we’re doing a tour, just around the U.K. for now, although we did just play in Greece which was lovely. And that, we’re sort of trying to line up all the dates within October and November because the drummer then goes off on tour for about six months after that. So with that project it’s very much, that is dependent on people’s availability. But actually with Satori I often book, I often book dates hoping that everyone is free. But often James Maddren isn’t, he’s away a lot of the time. And I have a couple of wonderful set drummers and so it still sounds like a band and that music is kind of free and spontaneous enough for it to be someone can sort of step in and do their thing rather than need to sound like James Maddren which wouldn’t be really what I want somebody to feel like they have to do.
Yeah, and as you said, you mentioned the one drummer that was playing on “Insomnia” I guess and that they brought something to the table that someone else might not have.

Yeah. Absolutely. And I think that’s what I’m looking for really in band members is somebody that can complement what I’ve written but also really be able to do their own thing and interpret the music, so they’ll come up with ideas that I never would have considered. And then it will go in a different direction and it very much feels like a band rather than I’m the sole composer of this piece of music and anyone can come in and just play it note for note. But that’s something that jazz musicians --
